transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-30
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood), Jordan Miles (Oakridge VP Eng), Sofia Park (Cloud Architect), Liam O'Connor (Security), Renee Zhao (SRE)

Summary (auto): intake discovery to validate Oakridge's private deployment requirements for Redwood Private. Topics: VPC topology, peering vs private endpoints, transit gateway/transit hub design, region gating (EU residency), IP/CIDR overlap, KMS and audit logs, SSO/SAML, timeline for pilot.

Topics:
- Private endpoints vs VPC peering tradeoffs
- Transit gateway and egress designs
- Region constraints (EU-only workloads)
- Security controls (KMS, SOC 2, RBAC)
- Next steps and network workshop

Transcript:
00:00:03 Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh appreciate you taking time. we, we wanted to do a quick run through of Oakridge's target topology and make sure we understand any blockers for a Private deployment.
00:00:15 Jordan Miles: Yeah thanks Alex. Quick intro, I'm Jordan, VP Eng, Sofia is our cloud architect, Liam leads security, Renee is our SRE. We're evaluating Redwood because the latency numbers look promising but our concern is the private onramp and region restrictions.
00:00:30 Priya Nair: Great. One quick note: when folks say "Private" with Redwood we mean the Private control plane option that can be deployed in your VPC with private endpoints. there is also Dedicated which is reserved capacity — sorry if we're using different words — 
00:00:46 Jordan Miles: Right, that's the first question: do we have to peer to Redwood VPC or can we use Private endpoints into our VPC? We have strict egress rules and no cross-account peered routes unless it's approved.
00:01:01 Priya Nair: Good question. Both patterns are supported. We typically recommend Private endpoints for customers wanting minimal routing changes — they use interface endpoints and keep traffic within the VPC. Peering is an option, but peering requires CIDR planning and transitive routing tends to be blocked unless you use a transit gateway.
00:01:20 Sofia Park: So the interface endpoint model — that means we still talk to a Redwood private load balancer in our account? how does the control plane work, like where are the service endpoints deployed?
00:01:34 Samir Patel: Yes, with Private we push a small control plane into your account or VPC — it's a lightweight control plane that handles model versioning and rollout. networking-wise we create interface endpoints, or you can configure a transit gateway attachment for higher throughput. sometimes the transcript generator calls it Redwood "Dedicate" or "Redwood Dedicatee" so sorry for earlier docs.
00:01:54 Liam O'Connor: Are we able to keep traffic entirely in-region for EU residents? regulatory constraint: EU-only inference for a subset of models and customer data. We cannot have tokens or request metadata leave eu-west-1.
00:02:10 Priya Nair: We can pin model routing by region. Redwood Private supports region gating — you can restrict certain projects or routes to eu-west-1 nodes. There are some caveats around fallback: if a region is out of capacity we can automatically fall back to other compatible model variants in-region if available, otherwise you'd want to set a strict no-fallback policy.
00:02:30 Jordan Miles: Fallback isn't acceptable for some EU workloads. So we want hard routing. What's the SLA if we do that?
00:02:38 Alex Chen: With Private, SLAs are part of the Enterprise contract — for strict in-region pinning we work with your infra team to ensure capacity is reserved (similar to Dedicated but inside your VPC). we'll capture that in the pilot scoping.
00:02:50 Renee Zhao: On IP/CIDR, we have limited address space and several services that already use the 10.0.0.0/16. We can't overlap. What's the recommendation?
00:03:03 Priya Nair: We'd ask for an isolated VPC or a dedicated subnet block for Redwood endpoints. We also have a sample Terraform that shows /24s for interface endpoints and a small management subnet for the control plane. I'll share that.
00:03:20 Sofia Park: If we go transit gateway for higher throughput, do we need to open egress to the internet? Our security posture is no outbound unless through egress firewall.
00:03:33 Samir Patel: For transit gateway attachments, traffic stays within your transit hub. Egress to public internet is only required if you choose a hosted model or enable telemetry back to Redwood's hosted control plane. For Private you can opt for a fully air-gapped flow — but some features like automatic model updates or metrics ingestion may require outbound connection to specific endpoints; alternatively we can route through a proxy.
00:04:00 Liam O'Connor: KMS: we need CMKs in our AWS account for encrypting model artifacts and logs. Is that supported?
00:04:08 Priya Nair: Yes, customer-managed KMS is supported. Redwood can integrate with your CMKs and we can log key usage in CloudTrail. There might be some small bootstrap keys for the control plane but primary encryption at rest can be CMK-managed.
00:04:23 Jordan Miles: What about audit logs and retention? We have a 7-year retention for some audit trails.
00:04:29 Alex Chen: We ship audit logs into your CloudWatch or S3 depending on your preference. Retention can be configured on your side. We also offer a long-term retention add-on if you'd like Redwood to retain copies.
00:04:42 Sofia Park: Network ACLs and security groups — is there a list of ports we need to open?
00:04:48 Priya Nair: Yes, we provide a firewall spec: usually 443 outbound for API, a few internal ports for health and metrics (we'll send the exact list). For private endpoints we create ENIs so security groups need to allow the subnets your apps run in to talk to those ENIs.
00:05:00 Jordan Miles: What about SSO? We use SAML and SCIM provisioning.
00:05:05 Samir Patel: SSO via SAML is supported; SCIM provisioning for user sync is available on enterprise plans. RBAC can be mapped to your directory groups.
00:05:15 Liam O'Connor: Are there any known gotchas — like KV cash or things where the caching breaks with interface endpoints? we've seen odd token leakage with other vendors.
00:05:26 Priya Nair: Ha, KV cash — yes the transcriber loves to swap words. On a serious note, KV cache behavior is identical; the main thing to watch for is MTU and path MTU when you have deep inspection proxies — large token streams can be cut if the proxy re-assembles incorrectly. We recommend verifying your proxy and MTU settings.
00:05:47 Renee Zhao: Latency. If we host the control plane in eu-west-1 and model server is eu-west-1, what's the expected p50/p99?
00:05:55 Priya Nair: For typical open models: p50 sub-50ms for short completions and p99 depends on sequence length and batching. We can provide benchmark CSVs specific to your instance types. For strict SLOs you'd want reserved capacity.
00:06:10 Jordan Miles: Okay — procurement question: we have to validate vendor security posture. can you share SOC 2 and any penetration test reports?
00:06:18 Alex Chen: Absolutely. We'll send SOC 2 Type II and a summary of recent pentest findings. We'll also share a network hardening guide and our private deployment checklist.
00:06:28 Sofia Park: For the pilot, our idea is to route traffic for a single self-hosted model and run a perf test with 10QPS for 2 weeks. is that workable?
00:06:37 Priya Nair: Yes, that's exactly the kind of pilot we recommend. We'll help size the instance profiles and the burst vs steady throughput. We'll also outline data flow and E2E network diagrams.
00:06:48 Jordan Miles: Is there a recommended way for us to run end-to-end tracing? We use OpenTelemetry and need to correlate logs.
00:06:55 Samir Patel: We instrument for OpenTelemetry and can export traces to your tracing backend. We'll share tracing hooks and a small demo.
00:07:06 Liam O'Connor: Any compliance concerns for running models with PII?
00:07:11 Priya Nair: Redwood has a data handling policy; for Private deployments your data never leaves your VPC unless you opt into external telemetry. We'll put the specifics in the security doc.
00:07:20 Jordan Miles: Bandwidth: our private peering will go through a couple of customer NATs. Do you have egress numbers per token?
00:07:28 Alex Chen: We typically model tokens to bytes and have an estimate; Priya will attach a spreadsheet. It depends on encoding, response size, and frequency. For planning, we usually recommend headroom of 30% above estimated peak.
00:07:45 Renee Zhao: One more thing: IP whitelisting vs service endpoints. can we pre-authorize a known set of ENIs?
00:07:53 Priya Nair: For interface endpoints you can security-group restrict to the subnets and use AWS PrivateLink. For peering you'd whitelist CIDRs. If you need fixed IPs we can also support egress through a NAT with Elastic IPs in your account.
00:08:08 Jordan Miles: Great. I also want to ensure we limit fallback to other regions — we want fail-stop rather than fail-over for the EU project.
00:08:17 Alex Chen: Noted — we'll document a strict no-fallback policy for those routes. That will be part of the pilot SLA.
00:08:25 Sofia Park: Are there any sample VPC topologies you can share — like small/medium/large?
00:08:31 Priya Nair: Yes, small: interface endpoints + single subnet; medium: transit gateway with dedicated attachments; large: transit gateway, multiple AZs, reserved capacity pools. We'll share a network-deck link after the call.
00:08:45 Jordan Miles: Timeline wise we want to start pilot by mid-October. the SREs need to do an intake review and we need procurement paperwork.
00:08:54 Alex Chen: That feels doable. Action items we'll capture. We'll send an initial diagram and a Terraform example.
00:09:00 (crosstalk) Speaker 5: um can you also—
00:09:04 Priya Nair: Sorry who was that?
00:09:07 Speaker 5: Renee, my mistake.
00:09:10 Jordan Miles: Final ask: can Redwood do a quick 45-minute workshop for our network and SRE folks next week?
00:09:16 Priya Nair: Yes we'll set that up — Priya will own scheduling.
00:09:20 Alex Chen: I'll email SOC2 and KMS docs and a sample VPC template by Tuesday.
00:09:26 Jordan Miles: Perfect — thanks everyone.
00:09:30 Alex Chen: Thanks all.
